desc:
Among all strings of the minimum possible length that contain both a and b as subsequences, return the one that comes first in alphabetical (lexicographic) order.

If both inputs are empty, return the empty string.

a = "abac", b = "cab"  ->  "cabac"
a = "ab",   b = "ba"   ->  "aba"   ("bab" is as short but alphabetically later)
a = "",     b = "xy"   ->  "xy"
constraints: Both strings contain only lowercase English letters
hints: First find only the length of the shortest common supersequence. Let f(i, j) be that length for the suffixes a[i:] and b[j:].
f(i, j) = 1 + f(i+1, j+1) if a[i] == b[j], else 1 + min(f(i+1, j), f(i, j+1)). Fill the table from the end of both strings, with f(m, j) = n - j and f(i, n) = m - i.

Build the answer from the front. At (i, j): equal characters are always written once and both pointers advance. Otherwise write a[i] if moving to (i+1, j) keeps the length optimal, or b[j] if (i, j+1) does; when both keep it optimal, write the smaller of the two characters. Append the rest of the other string when one is used up.
editorial: Work with suffixes so the answer can be produced front to back. Let f[i][j] be the length of the shortest common supersequence of a[i:] and b[j:]. If a[i] == b[j], a shortest supersequence can always start with this letter shared by both strings, so f[i][j] = 1 + f[i+1][j+1]. Otherwise the first character of an optimal answer must be a[i] or b[j] (any other letter would be wasted), giving 1 + min(f[i+1][j], f[i][j+1]).

To make the result lexicographically smallest among strings of equal (minimum) length, decide each character greedily from the left, because with equal lengths the first differing character settles the order. At state (i, j): when the characters are equal, any optimal answer can start with that letter and advancing both pointers loses nothing, and no other first letter is possible. When they differ, the candidate first letters are a[i] (allowed only if f[i+1][j] + 1 == f[i][j]) and b[j] (allowed only if f[i][j+1] + 1 == f[i][j]). Two different letters can never tie, so we simply take the smaller allowed one, and the rest of the answer is the best answer from the new state.

When one string is used up, the remainder of the other is forced. The table costs O(m · n) time and memory, and the reconstruction is O(m + n). Writing any valid shortest supersequence is easier, but would not be unique, which is why the problem asks for the alphabetically smallest.
